summary.label: SUMMARY
summary.heading: I ask a lot of questions before I write code.
body: I'm a full-stack engineer. I spent two years writing production code at Programiz Pro, a coding-education platform with over 100,000 paid learners. I built the course flow APIs, the learner dashboard and the certificate engine, and I integrated Paddle, which every paid learner pays through. Most recently I led four engineers during my internship at Jobss.ai, on a Laravel job platform that's live in production. I was responsible for authentication, role-based access, the employer workspace and the marketplace search.

During my Master's I led a team of three that built two connected systems. One is a warehouse platform with a locking stock ledger in PostgreSQL. The other is a multi-tenant Next.js storefront with its own payment service. Day to day I work in React, Next.js, Node.js, TypeScript, PostgreSQL and Laravel.
Some of those questions sound obvious. I ask them anyway, because now and then the answer isn't what anyone assumed, and I'd rather find that out before the code exists.
I'm from Nepal and live in Melbourne, where I recently finished a Master's in Software Engineering. Outside work I read, travel when I can, and watch a lot of anime.

entries.product: Job and task distribution platform, live in production. Laravel and PHP, with Blade views built from Figma designs.
bullets: Led four engineers. I made the architecture decisions and reviewed every pull request before it merged.
Built authentication and role-based access control for four roles, all checked against one permission model.
Designed the employer workspace in Laravel and Blade. An employer posts a job or task there, then moves applicants through review, shortlist and rejection.
Marketplace search runs on a single index for both sides. Employers use it to find people, seekers use it to find work.
I picked cursor-based pagination over offset for the job and task feeds, because offset gets slower the deeper you page. Each feed is scoped to active dates.
Wrote the allocation logic that spreads available workers across open jobs and tasks based on demand.

entries.product: Coding-education platform behind programiz.com and programiz.pro, with over 100,000 paid learners.
bullets: Built the course flow APIs in Node.js, TypeScript and MySQL, and the learner dashboard on programiz.pro. Over 100,000 paid learners use them to work through and finish a course.
Integrated the Paddle payment API, which every paid learner pays through. I wrote the webhooks and the checkout iframe messaging, and Programiz still takes payment through that flow today.
Built the certificate engine in Node.js and TypeScript. It has issued over 100,000 verified completion certificates.

Owned the online compiler on programiz.com, which gets around 23 million visits a month from Google search. Python output was arriving over the socket in pieces. With the principal engineer, I fixed it with a heartbeat that joins the pieces into one response.
Led a team of six on Programiz Reports, a feature for beginners learning to program. We went from the content team's requirements to release in two weeks.
Integrated sensAI, an LLM-backed tutor, into the exercise page. Learners ask it over 300 questions a day.
Wrote end-to-end tests in Playwright and Cypress and ran them in GitHub Actions CI.
Added Mixpanel and Microsoft Clarity to the landing pages, then rewrote the pages based on what people actually did on them.

entries.name: Nexus: warehouse management platform
entries.description: My team of three built this during my Master's. I run an anime-apparel side business where stock kept going missing and I packed every order by hand, and Nexus is the system I wanted for it. It syncs stock and order state with Aroma.
bullets: Modelled the warehouse as a labelled tree, so I can look up any item's exact location in seconds.
Product drops run through a state machine covering supplier onboarding, lot negotiation, intake and lot-level pricing. A drop can't jump a stage.
Designed the stock ledger in PostgreSQL. It locks rows with SELECT FOR UPDATE, so two buyers can't claim the same unit.
Built lot-aware replenishment with a return-to-order path. A refund or exchange puts the stock back in the correct inventory state.
Designed the fulfilment pipeline. Cron jobs batch retail orders, and each order is its own state machine, tracked until it completes.
I'm now rebuilding it as e-warehouse with an agentic workflow in Claude Code. I write the specs, agents implement them, and I review every change.

codeNote.text: The repo is private because it runs a live side business. I can walk you through the data model and the state machines.

entries.name: Aroma: multi-tenant clothing e-commerce
entries.description: Built alongside Nexus by the same team. A multi-tenant storefront where sellers run their own shop on shared infrastructure.
bullets: Designed the tenancy model. Each seller gets an isolated storefront, and all of them run on one shared backend.
Specified checkout to reserve stock when an order is confirmed. An idempotency key stops a retry from creating a duplicate order.
Moved payments into their own service, with the eSewa and Khalti gateways behind one interface.
Orders go to Nexus through a shared Redis instance, with REST as the fallback. The catalogue is cached in Redis too.
Designed the buyer path in Next.js: search, product pages, cart, reservation, checkout and order history.

Catalogue pages use server rendering and static generation because they need to be indexed and load fast. Anything per-user is fetched on the client, with React Query holding the cache and Zustand holding the cart.
Ran Lighthouse on the product details page. Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) came in under two seconds.
Added an order-status view so buyers can track an order after paying. Sellers who only sell through social media can't offer that.

codeNote.text: The repo is private. It hasn't launched yet and it's wired into Nexus. Happy to walk through the tenancy model and how I split rendering.

earlier.name: Hospital E-Ticketing
earlier.summary: Hospitals and doctors register on the platform and open weekly appointment slots, and patients book online. The backend uses an inversion-test algorithm to stop double bookings across the Doctor, Patient and Hospital Admin roles.

earlier.name: Futsal Finder
earlier.summary: Tinder-style matchmaking for competitive futsal teams, as an Android app built in Kotlin. Teams set their preferences and get matched with nearby opponents and venues. It also had league and knockout tournaments, tiered battle seasons and court booking. This was the first full system I built.

aiEngineering.label: AGENTIC ENGINEERING
aiEngineering.heading: How I work with AI agents
intro: I run my development through AI coding agents, and I keep the decisions. I decide what gets built, write the spec it's built against, and review what comes back.

Nexus and Aroma were built this way by a team of three I led. I wrote the spikes and specs, AI models implemented against them, and I reviewed every pull request, over 400 in two years. Below is what I'm building now, the setup I use, and the skills I built for it.

blocks.heading: e-warehouse
body: A web app for clothing merchants. Version 1 is an age-aware lot ledger. Each batch of stock, called a lot, is recorded with its variants, quantities and arrival date, so the merchant always knows how old the stock is.

Clothes don't rot. They go out of season. So every lot gets a market-level expiry date, the date it should be sold by. The bigger idea is a timeline where the merchant sketches each lot's life from ordered to closed, with notes like "the offer should have started on 25 Sep". When a lot closes, those lessons carry into the next order. The merchant makes the calls, and the app only guides.

items.name: Backend
items.text: The skeleton is built and merged. It starts, validates its settings, connects to Postgres, reports its health and shuts down cleanly. There are no product features yet, and no tests yet either. That's on purpose, and ADR 0006 says why.

items.name: Architecture
items.text: Ten decision records so far. Express stays at the edge, so business logic never imports it. The whole API shares one response envelope and a fixed set of error codes. Every response and log line carries a request ID. Stock changes are stored as new rows and never edited in place.

items.name: Design
items.text: Designed, not built. I had Claude Design generate four directions on the same data, picked one, and refined it over two more rounds, with three options only for the two parts I was unsure about. Then I ran a design psychology audit. UX calls trace back to growth.design case studies and named principles such as Hick's law and the endowment effect.

items.name: Scope
items.text: I work in Musk's order: question, delete, simplify, accelerate, automate. The warehouse map, rooms and pricing are parked until the lot ledger proves itself. On 2 Oct a review showed the product had drifted into a layout builder. On 3 Oct I pulled it back to the ledger and moved maps to version 2.

items.name: Users
items.text: None yet. My own business check flagged that no merchant has confirmed the problem, so it's written in the decision log where I can't ignore it.

items.name: Records
items.text: 11 merged pull requests since 13 Sep 2026, a dated log of every product decision with its source, and a log of open questions.

notes: The frontend comes next, in Vite, React and TypeScript, desktop first. One pnpm check command is the definition of done, and a commit hook blocks secrets before they reach the repo.

codeNote.text: The repo is private. I can walk you through the ADRs and the decision log.

blocks.heading: The setup
blocks.meta: Tools I use, not tools I built
body: These are the tools I use every day.

items.name: Claude Code
items.text: My main coding agent. I moved to it from Pi in September 2026. Different models get different jobs: a light one explores the codebase, a stronger one drafts plans, and a mid-tier one writes the code.

items.name: Firstmate
items.text: Supervises several AI workers at once. Each one works in its own copy of the repo and delivers a pull request that I review and merge.

items.name: Lavish
items.text: Turns agent output into review pages. I answer design questions, pick options and leave notes on the page, and the agent picks them up.

items.name: Claude Design
items.text: Generates UI directions for me to choose between and refine.

items.name: Excalidraw
items.text: Where I sketch the structure of a problem before any code exists.

notes: Some decisions never go to an agent, and the project's instructions say so. I decide what gets built next. I write every spec and get grilled on it before any code. I do code review and merging. And I keep one-way doors, meaning anything expensive to undo, like a database table, the API's shape, deleting data, security or a new package. Two-way doors go fast. The e-warehouse design is frozen, but its new tables still wait for a spec.

Every handoff comes back with a receipt: the objective, what changed, what was verified, what wasn't, the risks and the approval needed. I review against the receipt instead of taking the agent's word that it's done.
When a mistake repeats, it moves down a ladder: first an explanation, then a checklist, a template, an automated check, and finally an enforced policy.

blocks.heading: Agent skills I built
body: A library of reusable skills my agents load when a task calls for one.

items.name: spec-driven
items.text: Decides first whether a feature needs a spec at all. If it does, it works through spike, reference, spec, test plan and running order, and grills me at each step.

items.name: chifuyu
items.text: An architecture reviewer built from the published work of Kun Chen, Matt Pocock and Kent C. Dodds. It weighs a change by its blast radius.

items.name: hunter-sung
items.text: A business check built from the published thinking of Jeff Bezos, Jamie Dimon, Satya Nadella, Lisa Su, Steve Jobs and Elon Musk. It asks whose problem this is, what we can drop, what the worst case is, and which number proves it worked. Every point cites its source.

items.name: kaizen
items.text: Keeps work to one task at a time, with a Now, Next and Parked list.

items.name: project-map
items.text: Keeps each project's map of where information lives.

items.name: clean-code
items.text: 145 rules from Robert C. Martin's Clean Code, rewritten for TypeScript and React after I read all 462 pages. My own engineering rules win in the 8 places they disagree.

items.name: ew-code
items.text: e-warehouse's own code rules in one skill. It replaced 19 separate rule files.

notes: clean-code is split into one file per topic, so an agent loads only the rules a task needs. A naming-only task went from about 7,400 tokens to about 2,200. When agents do most of the reading, that's a real cost saving.

The library also revises itself. A hook logs every time a skill is used. After 20 uses, 30 days or any feedback, a skill comes up for review, and a fresh agent drafts the changes, each one backed by evidence from real uses.
